title: A 50MB file is in your history forever
summary: Someone committed a binary blob. Deleting it does nothing to the clone size. Find the offender, measure the damage, and understand what LFS would have done instead.
mental_model: Every version of every file ever committed lives in the object database forever. Deleting a file only stops it appearing in new commits — the blob stays, and every clone downloads it.

setup.run: sh -c 'head -c 900000 /dev/urandom | base64 > assets/sample-tank.raw 2>/dev/null || (mkdir -p assets && head -c 900000 /dev/urandom | base64 > assets/sample-tank.raw)'
git commit -q -m "Remove the sample capture, it was a mistake"

steps.title: The file is gone — and the repository is not smaller
steps.why: The working tree is clean of it and HEAD does not contain it. Yet the object database still holds every byte, because a commit in the middle of history does.
steps.expect: No assets directory, but a size-pack far larger than the source warrants.

steps.title: List every object with its size
steps.why: `rev-list --objects --all` enumerates every object in history with its path; `cat-file --batch-check` reports each one's type and size. Piped together, they are the standard repository-forensics tool.
commands: sh -c 'git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check="%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)" | grep ^blob | sort -k3 -rn | head -5'
steps.expect: The capture file at the top, by a wide margin.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check="%(objecttype) %(objectsize) %(rest)" | grep ^blob | sort -k2 -rn | head -1'
verify.label: the largest blob in history is identifiable

steps.title: Find which commits carry it
steps.why: Knowing the path, `log --diff-filter` tells you when it arrived and when it left. Both commits still contain it in their trees — that is why it cannot simply be forgotten.

verify.label: two commits touch the file: the add and the delete

steps.title: Prove garbage collection will not save you
steps.why: `gc` only removes unreachable objects. This blob is reachable from a commit on main, so it is not garbage — it is history. Nothing short of rewriting that commit removes it.
steps.expect: Barely any change: the blob is reachable and therefore kept.

verify.label: the blob is still reachable after gc
verify.hint: gc removes unreachable objects only — this one is in a commit

steps.title: See what a clone actually costs
steps.why: A fresh clone downloads the whole reachable object set, including the blob nobody wants. Every colleague, every CI run, every container build pays for it.
steps.expect: The clone is large despite the working tree being small.

steps.title: Set up what should have happened: LFS-style pointers
steps.why: Git LFS replaces a big file with a small text pointer in git, storing the bytes elsewhere. `.gitattributes` marks which paths are handled that way — the mechanism is exactly the filter system git already has.

write.content:
# Binary captures go to LFS, never into the object database.
assets/**/*.raw filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
*.psd filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
*.mp4 filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text

commands: git commit -q -m "Route binary assets through LFS"
steps.expect: check-attr reports filter: lfs for that path.

verify.label: large binaries are routed to LFS from now on
verify.hint: add an LFS filter rule to .gitattributes

steps.title: Know the only real cure
steps.why: Removing an existing blob means rewriting every commit that contains it — `git filter-repo`, new shas, a force push, and every clone re-made. Prevention through .gitattributes and a pre-commit size check is enormously cheaper.
steps.expect: Nothing rewritten here — the rewriting category covers that operation properly.

verify.label: the large blob is still in history, as expected
verify.hint: deleting a file does not remove it from past commits

verify.label: …even though it is not in the current tree
an LFS rule now covers that path for future commits
the rule is committed so it applies to everyone

pitfalls: `git rm` and `git gc` do not shrink a repository whose blob is reachable from history. Only a rewrite does.
Adding LFS afterwards protects future commits only; existing blobs stay until history is rewritten with `git lfs migrate` or `git filter-repo`.
Without the LFS client installed, a checkout gives you pointer text files instead of content. Everyone on the project needs it.
A pre-commit hook rejecting files over a few megabytes prevents the entire problem for the cost of ten lines of shell.
